title: NUMA Hit/Miss Ratio Tracking
exclusions: Calculates a host-wide ratio from positive deltas of the Linux kernel's cumulative `numa_hit` and `numa_miss` normal-page counters exposed in `/sys/devices/system/node/node*/numastat`. It does not measure memory-access latency, bandwidth, CPU-cache misses, current page residency, per-process locality, page migration, huge-page allocation, or application impact; identify the process or policy responsible; change NUMA placement; or provide security or regulatory assurance. Host aggregation can hide one poorly behaving node, so use a per-node detector when node attribution is required. Memoryless-node topologies are rejected because kernel documentation warns that they can heavily skew the counters. The primary report labels active exact-host exceptions but preserves their rows, and a separate inventory-backed freshness control is required to detect a completely silent host.
evidence: For an implemented deployment, retain the `linux_numa_hit_ratio_tracking` base-report export, the `linux_numa_hit_ratio_alert` definition and scheduler history, raw `linux:numastat` events spanning the baseline and evaluation window, the collector file and hash, effective `inputs.conf` and `props.conf`, same-poll sysfs or default-`numastat` comparisons, threshold approval, exception-lookup revision, and result rows containing `_time`, `host`, `numa_hit_pages`, `numa_miss_pages`, `hit_miss_pages`, `hit_pct`, `miss_pct`, `numa_foreign_pages`, `foreign_miss_gap_pages`, `complete_intervals`, `covered_seconds`, `expected_node_count`, `sample_age_seconds`, and `disposition`. Those artifacts demonstrate source and rule behavior; this documentation-only review did not execute the collector or SPL, establish performance impact, or produce runtime evidence.

controlTest.positiveScenario: In a temporary index, create 13 one-minute-apart `event_version=1 collector=numastat_counter_v1 event_type=node_sample collection_status=ok topology_status=qualified` samples ending in complete minutes for each of two nodes on `host=numa-hit-positive`, with one fixed valid `boot_id` and `expected_node_count=2`. Start every counter at a nonnegative value. On each of the 12 transitions, add 445 `numa_hit`, 55 `numa_miss`, 55 `numa_foreign`, 0 `interleave_hit`, 445 `local_node`, and 55 `other_node` pages per node. Run the SPL with only the temporary index substituted. Expect one host row with `complete_intervals=12`, `covered_seconds=720`, `numa_hit_pages=10680`, `numa_miss_pages=1320`, `hit_miss_pages=12000`, `hit_pct=89.0`, `miss_pct=11.0`, and `disposition=investigate`. Add an unexpired exact-host lookup row: the base report must retain the row as `approved_test`, while the alert derivative ending in `| where disposition="investigate"` must return zero rows.
controlTest.negativeScenario: Create the same complete two-node fixture on `host=numa-hit-negative`, but add 450 `numa_hit`, 50 `numa_miss`, 50 `numa_foreign`, 0 `interleave_hit`, 450 `local_node`, and 50 `other_node` pages per node on each transition. Expect zero rows because the calculated hit percentage is exactly 90.0 and the policy is strictly below 90. In separate runs, decrease any cumulative counter or change `boot_id` on the seventh sample; that transition must be discarded, leaving only 11 valid complete intervals and therefore zero rows. Also verify zero rows for a denominator below 1,000 pages, one absent node, a declared node-count disagreement, a gap over 180 seconds, a collector-error event, or a counter above Splunk's exact-integer guard.

dataSources: A locally managed Splunk Universal Forwarder scripted input reads `/sys/devices/system/node/node*/numastat`, each node's `meminfo`, and `/proc/sys/kernel/random/boot_id` every 60 seconds. It sends one key-value event per qualified regular-memory NUMA node to the deployment-selected `index=os` with local `sourcetype=linux:numastat`; classified collector errors use the same source type. Required sample fields are `event_version`, `collector`, `event_type`, `collection_status`, `topology_status`, `numa_node`, `expected_node_count`, `boot_id`, `numa_hit`, `numa_miss`, `numa_foreign`, `interleave_hit`, `local_node`, and `other_node`; `_time`, `host`, and `source` are Splunk metadata. The six counters are cumulative counts of normal memory pages, not bytes or rates. This source contract is custom and is not supplied by the Splunk Add-on for Unix and Linux.
app: Splunk Universal Forwarder native scripted input packaged in a locally maintained deployment app such as `TA_linux_numastat_counters`. No Splunkbase app, premium Splunk app, modular input, HEC token, or `Splunk_TA_nix` input supplies this custom source type.

index=os sourcetype="linux:numastat" earliest=-16m@m latest=@m
| eventstats count(eval(event_type="collector_error" OR collection_status="error")) as collector_error_events by host
| eval event_time=_time, event_version=tonumber(event_version), numa_node=tonumber(numa_node), expected_node_count=tonumber(expected_node_count), boot_id=lower(boot_id), numa_hit=tonumber(numa_hit), numa_miss=tonumber(numa_miss), numa_foreign=tonumber(numa_foreign), interleave_hit=tonumber(interleave_hit), local_node=tonumber(local_node), other_node=tonumber(other_node)

| eventstats max(event_time) as latest_event_time by host numa_node _time
| where event_time=latest_event_time
| stats latest(event_time) as sample_time latest(boot_id) as boot_id latest(numa_hit) as numa_hit latest(numa_miss) as numa_miss latest(numa_foreign) as numa_foreign latest(interleave_hit) as interleave_hit latest(local_node) as local_node latest(other_node) as other_node dc(boot_id) as boot_ids dc(expected_node_count) as declared_node_counts latest(expected_node_count) as expected_node_count by host numa_node _time
| where boot_ids=1 AND declared_node_counts=1
| sort 0 host numa_node _time
| streamstats current=f window=1 last(_time) as previous_bucket last(boot_id) as previous_boot_id last(numa_hit) as previous_numa_hit last(numa_miss) as previous_numa_miss last(numa_foreign) as previous_numa_foreign last(interleave_hit) as previous_interleave_hit last(local_node) as previous_local_node last(other_node) as previous_other_node by host numa_node
| eval interval_seconds=_time-previous_bucket, numa_hit_delta=numa_hit-previous_numa_hit, numa_miss_delta=numa_miss-previous_numa_miss, numa_foreign_delta=numa_foreign-previous_numa_foreign, interleave_hit_delta=interleave_hit-previous_interleave_hit, local_node_delta=local_node-previous_local_node, other_node_delta=other_node-previous_other_node
| where _time>=relative_time(now(),"-15m@m") AND boot_id=previous_boot_id AND interval_seconds>0 AND interval_seconds<=180 AND numa_hit_delta>=0 AND numa_miss_delta>=0 AND numa_foreign_delta>=0 AND interleave_hit_delta>=0 AND local_node_delta>=0 AND other_node_delta>=0

| where declared_node_counts=1 AND observed_node_count=expected_node_count AND interval_span_variants=1
| stats sum(interval_numa_hit_pages) as numa_hit_pages sum(interval_numa_miss_pages) as numa_miss_pages sum(interval_numa_foreign_pages) as numa_foreign_pages sum(interval_interleave_hit_pages) as interleave_hit_pages sum(interval_local_node_pages) as local_node_pages sum(interval_other_node_pages) as other_node_pages sum(interval_seconds) as covered_seconds count as complete_intervals dc(expected_node_count) as declared_node_counts latest(expected_node_count) as expected_node_count latest(sample_time) as _time by host
| eval hit_miss_pages=numa_hit_pages+numa_miss_pages, cpu_observed_pages=local_node_pages+other_node_pages
| where declared_node_counts=1 AND complete_intervals>=12 AND covered_seconds>=720 AND hit_miss_pages>=1000
| eval hit_pct=round(100*numa_hit_pages/hit_miss_pages,1), miss_pct=round(100*numa_miss_pages/hit_miss_pages,1), foreign_miss_gap_pages=abs(numa_foreign_pages-numa_miss_pages), other_node_pct=if(cpu_observed_pages>0,round(100*other_node_pages/cpu_observed_pages,1),null()), sample_age_seconds=now()-_time
| where hit_pct<90
| lookup linux_numa_hit_ratio_exceptions.csv host OUTPUT valid_until_epoch change_id reason
| eval valid_until_epoch=tonumber(valid_until_epoch), disposition=if(isnotnull(change_id) AND valid_until_epoch>=now(),"approved_test","investigate")
| table _time host expected_node_count numa_hit_pages numa_miss_pages hit_miss_pages hit_pct miss_pct numa_foreign_pages foreign_miss_gap_pages interleave_hit_pages local_node_pages other_node_pages other_node_pct complete_intervals covered_seconds sample_age_seconds disposition change_id reason
| sort 0 hit_pct host
description: Reports a host when at least 12 complete, topology-consistent counter intervals cover 12 minutes or more within the last 15 complete minutes, at least 1,000 hit-plus-miss pages were observed, and positive cumulative deltas produce a host-wide NUMA allocation-policy hit percentage below 90. It rejects reboot/reset transitions, incomplete node sets, collection errors, long gaps, and numerically unsafe counters while preserving companion statistics and exception disposition for investigation.
value: A sustained drop in preferred-node allocation success can reveal placement, memory-policy, or node-capacity conditions before teams make speculative tuning changes. Window deltas prevent historical lifetime activity from dominating the result, and the boot, topology, volume, and coverage guards make the signal more defensible than summing raw cumulative counters. Host aggregation provides a stable fleet view, while retained companion counters help engineers decide whether per-node and process-level investigation is warranted.
implementation: Deploy the documented `numastat_counter_v1` read-only collector at 60-second intervals and verify all six page counters against the same poll's node sysfs files or the default `numastat` display. Schedule `linux_numa_hit_ratio_tracking` every five minutes over the last 15 complete minutes plus a baseline minute. Start with at least 12 complete intervals, 720 covered seconds, 1,000 hit-plus-miss pages, and `hit_pct<90`; treat those as local policy rather than vendor defaults, baseline by topology and workload, monitor source freshness separately, and notify only on `disposition=investigate`.
visualization: Use a 24-hour line chart of host `hit_pct` with a clearly labeled 90-percent local-policy line, paired with a latest-results table showing hit and miss delta pages, denominator, miss percentage, foreign/miss gap, companion other-node percentage, complete intervals, covered seconds, expected nodes, sample age, disposition, and change ID. Add a fleet heatmap by host and time plus separate panels for collector errors, missing expected hosts, topology rejection, counter-reset transitions, and low-volume windows. Label the ratio `allocation-policy hit percentage` and the counters `normal pages`; do not label them remote-memory latency, bytes, CPU-cache hits, or application slowdown. Drill down to raw node samples and the NUMA investigation runbook.
dataModelAcceleration: Not applicable. `linux:numastat` is a local operational counter contract with no claimed CIM mapping, and the search must order raw cumulative samples before calculating reset-safe deltas.

knownFalsePositives:
Every qualifying result is a real calculation over accepted kernel-counter increments. "False positive" means the condition is expected, not harmful, or unsuitable for the host class—not that a low ratio proves remote-access latency or an application fault.

1. **Approved NUMA policy or placement experiment** — `numactl --membind`, `--preferred`, or an `mbind(2)`/`set_mempolicy(2)` test can intentionally alter preferred-node allocation and drive misses. Match the host, command or service policy, test owner, ticket, and bounded UTC interval; inspect the test process's `/proc/<pid>/numa_maps`. Preserve the report as test evidence and suppress only notification with an expiring exact-host exception.

2. **Database, JVM, virtual-machine, or analytics startup** — Large first-touch allocation during startup, cache warm-up, failover, restore, or worker fan-out can briefly lower the 15-minute host ratio even when steady-state objectives remain healthy. Correlate the exact window with the named service event and compare later runs. If the behavior is accepted and repeatable, establish a workload-class threshold or bounded deployment window instead of a permanent host exclusion.

3. **Container or service cpuset mismatch by design** — Kubernetes, systemd, and batch schedulers can constrain allowed CPUs and memory nodes differently. A low preferred-allocation success rate may be consistent with that reviewed design. Compare effective `cpuset.cpus`/`cpuset.mems`, service affinity, process policy, and node pressure; correct unintended placement or document a reviewed threshold without treating an orchestrator name as sufficient suppression.

4. **Planned maintenance or memory-pressure exercise** — A capacity, failover, chaos, or resilience test may deliberately pressure an intended node and cause fallback. Verify the approved envelope, safety controls, stop time, and recovery in later windows. Continued degradation after the test expires remains actionable even when the initial cause was authorized.

5. **Host aggregation masks opposing node behavior** — A busy healthy node can contribute enough hits to dilute heavy misses on another node, while a low-traffic node can contribute too little to affect the fleet view. This is a known interpretation limit, not permission to average per-node percentages. Drill down to node delta counts or the separate per-node NUMA allocation-miss use case before deciding that all nodes are healthy.

6. **Topology or telemetry defect** — Memory hotplug, an unqualified memoryless node, duplicate scripted stanzas, stale source-type configuration, delayed events, or a collector version mismatch can make a ratio operationally untrustworthy. The primary SPL rejects known errors and incomplete intervals, while the separate health panel must expose them. Repair collection or requalify topology; never lower the 90-percent threshold to hide a data-quality problem.

**Suppression contract:** create `linux_numa_hit_ratio_exceptions.csv` with headers `host,valid_until_epoch,change_id,reason`. Require the exact Splunk host, UTC epoch seconds, one accountable change ID, no wildcard rows, and a bounded expiry. Restrict lookup writes and retain revisions. The base report classifies active rows as `approved_test` but does not remove them; derive the notification search by appending `| where disposition="investigate"`.

detailedImplementation:
## Prerequisites and semantic contract

Assign a Linux performance owner, a Splunk collection owner, and a search-content owner. The forwarder service account needs read and traverse access to `/sys/devices/system/node/node*/numastat`, the corresponding `meminfo` files, and `/proc/sys/kernel/random/boot_id`, plus its normal outbound forwarding route. Test those reads as that account. Do not grant root, `CAP_SYS_ADMIN`, memory-policy capabilities, or write access to sysfs merely to collect these read-only counters. The search owner needs read access to the chosen operating-system event index and controlled permission to create a report, an alert, and an exception lookup. `index=os`, the app and source-type names, field contract, thresholds, and saved-search names on this page are deployment conventions rather than Linux or Splunk defaults.

Define the signal before deployment. Linux exposes `numa_hit`, `numa_miss`, `numa_foreign`, `interleave_hit`, `local_node`, and `other_node` for every node in `/sys/devices/system/node/nodeN/numastat`; every value is a cumulative count of normal pages, while huge pages use separate counters. `numa_hit` increments on the preferred node when allocation succeeds there. If allocation succeeds elsewhere, `numa_foreign` increments on the preferred node and `numa_miss` increments on the node that supplied memory. The preferred node is often CPU-local, but an explicit memory policy can change it. `local_node` and `other_node` instead describe whether the allocating CPU and supplied memory share a node. Consequently, this use case calls `100*delta(numa_hit)/(delta(numa_hit)+delta(numa_miss))` the host allocation-policy hit percentage. It is not a CPU-cache hit rate, a byte ratio, or measured remote-memory latency.

Default `numastat` presents these kernel statistics per node in pages. Options such as `-n` alter units and formatting, so the automation reads the stable sysfs files directly and uses the command only for a same-time human check. Do not collect `/proc/zoneinfo` for this rule: it is neither the documented source of these six counters nor a substitute field contract. The kernel also warns that systems with CPU-bearing memoryless nodes can heavily skew the policy counters. The supplied collector rejects a topology whenever a discovered node lacks positive regular memory; an engineer must qualify such hardware separately rather than silently omitting the node.

## Step 1 — Package and configure collection

Place `scriptExample` at `$SPLUNK_HOME/etc/apps/TA_linux_numastat_counters/bin/collect_numastat_counters`, owned by the deployment account and executable by the Universal Forwarder service. The first pass discovers node counter files and confirms that every discovered node has a numeric, positive `MemTotal`. If no node exists, the boot UUID is malformed, or discovered and qualified counts differ, the script emits one classified `collector_error` and exits successfully so the failure itself can be indexed. The second pass emits one `node_sample` line per readable node only when all six named counters are present and nonnegative decimal integers; a missing or unreadable value becomes an error event, never zero.

`boot_id` identifies the running kernel instance. It lets the SPL reject the transition across a reboot rather than interpreting smaller post-boot cumulative counters as activity. `expected_node_count` lets every interval prove that all qualified nodes contributed. The script does not emit `host`; Splunk metadata remains authoritative for that identity. It deliberately preserves page counts and does not multiply by an assumed page size. If a responder needs bytes, obtain the relevant system page size for that host outside this rule and document the conversion.

Configure the input in `$SPLUNK_HOME/etc/apps/TA_linux_numastat_counters/local/inputs.conf`:

```ini
[script://$SPLUNK_HOME/etc/apps/TA_linux_numastat_counters/bin/collect_numastat_counters]
disabled = 0
interval = 60
index = os
sourcetype = linux:numastat
```

Leave `source` at the script-path default because it is useful provenance. Splunk documents that a scripted input indexes standard output, sends standard error to `splunkd.log`, and schedules the next interval relative to script completion. A continuously connected two-node host therefore produces about 2,880 sample events per day, not an exact wall-clock guarantee. On the parsing tier configure `[linux:numastat]` with `SHOULD_LINEMERGE = false` and `DATETIME_CONFIG = CURRENT`; the line has no source timestamp. On the search tier set `KV_MODE = auto` for key-value extraction. Apply settings on the correct tiers for the topology and restart the affected forwarder after input changes. No inbound listener, API credential, premium app, HEC endpoint, CIM acceleration, numactl package, or Splunk Add-on for Unix and Linux input is required.

Run the script manually as the forwarder account before deployment. Expect exactly one successful line per qualified node and one stable boot UUID. Immediately compare every emitted value with the same node's sysfs file; counters change under workload, so a comparison made minutes later is not an exact test. Run `splunk btool inputs list --debug` and confirm one winning stanza, the expected script path, 60-second interval, index, and source type. Duplicate stanzas are a collection fault because two samples can distort minute selection and increase ingest.

## Step 2 — Qualify fields, topology, and source health

Search `index=os sourcetype="linux:numastat" earliest=-15m` and inspect `_raw` with every field in `requiredFields`. Each active node should produce approximately one event a minute. Confirm that `event_version=1`, `collector=numastat_counter_v1`, successful rows have `event_type=node_sample`, `collection_status=ok`, and `topology_status=qualified`, and every counter is a nonnegative integer. Within one boot, cumulative values should not decrease. Compare the node IDs and `expected_node_count` with `/sys/devices/system/node/online` and each node's positive `MemTotal`; confirm against the platform hardware inventory and record or exclude any changing, memoryless, or ambiguous topology.

Where numactl is already installed, run default `numastat` at the same time and compare its per-node page values. Do not use `numastat -m`, which reports meminfo-style memory use, or `numastat -n`, which changes the display to megabytes. Small differences between sequential reads are expected on an allocating system; field identity, order of magnitude, and monotonic direction must agree. Preserve the direct sysfs comparison because sysfs is the collector's machine contract.

Create a separate freshness and collector-health search joined to the authoritative host inventory. It must identify expected hosts with no recent `node_sample` or `collector_error`, hosts reporting any `error_code`, changing declared node counts, and expected nodes missing for multiple polls. The ratio SPL intentionally suppresses a host that has a collector error and cannot discover a host that sends nothing. Never translate missing telemetry into a 100-percent hit rate or present a rejected host as healthy.

Splunk arithmetic converts fields to numeric values. The primary SPL caps every cumulative counter at 9,007,199,254,740,991 (2^53-1), the largest integer exactly representable by binary64-style arithmetic. A host beyond that guard belongs in the source-health queue until the numeric representation and delta strategy are redesigned; rounding a lifetime counter before subtraction can fabricate page deltas.

## Step 3 — Create and understand the saved searches

Save the primary SPL as `linux_numa_hit_ratio_tracking` and schedule it every five minutes. Its embedded `earliest=-16m@m latest=@m` selects a baseline minute plus 15 complete evaluation minutes and excludes the still-arriving current minute. It first counts collector-error events per host and validates the exact source contract. `bin` and the `latest_event_time` filter retain the newest sample for each host, node, and minute without allowing a retry to count as another interval.

**Understanding the delta logic:** after ordering each host/node series, `streamstats current=f window=1` attaches the preceding minute's boot ID and counters. The SPL subtracts cumulative values only when the boot UUID is unchanged, the interval is positive and no longer than 180 seconds, and every one of the six deltas is nonnegative. A reboot, reset, node re-creation, malformed event, or excessive gap therefore creates no artificial hit or miss contribution. The next aggregation forms a host interval only when every expected node contributes and all nodes use the same interval span. This prevents one missing node or mismatched coverage from biasing a host-wide ratio.

The final aggregation requires at least 12 complete intervals, at least 720 covered seconds, and at least 1,000 newly counted hit-plus-miss pages. The ratio uses sums of page deltas: `hit_pct=100*numa_hit_pages/(numa_hit_pages+numa_miss_pages)`. Never average node percentages, because a nearly idle node would receive the same weight as a busy node. `miss_pct` is the arithmetic complement subject to one-decimal rounding. `numa_foreign_pages` should broadly corroborate misses across a fully observed host, but sequential node reads can create boundary differences; `foreign_miss_gap_pages` is retained as a data-quality clue rather than required to equal zero. `other_node_pct` is a separate CPU-locality companion and is not substituted into the hit policy.

The initial alert policy is strictly `hit_pct<90`, not less than or equal to 90. Twelve intervals, 720 seconds, 1,000 pages, the 15-minute evaluation window, five-minute schedule, and 90-percent boundary are catalogue starting points. Baseline them by hardware, kernel line, virtual topology, workload class, and memory policy. Record every threshold change with owner, rationale, date, and repeated boundary tests.

Create `linux_numa_hit_ratio_exceptions.csv` exactly as documented in `knownFalsePositives`. Keep `linux_numa_hit_ratio_tracking` as the evidence-producing report with both dispositions. Clone it as `linux_numa_hit_ratio_alert`, append `| where disposition="investigate"`, and trigger when result count is greater than zero. Key any short throttle by `host` for no more than one normal schedule interval; use incident-state handling for persistence instead of an indefinite throttle that can hide an unresolved condition.

## Step 4 — Validate arithmetic and reset behavior

Load the positive and negative fixtures from `controlTest` into an isolated index with fixed event times in complete minute buckets. For the positive host, two nodes each add 445 hits and 55 misses over 12 transitions. Host totals are 10,680 hits and 1,320 misses, giving a 12,000-page denominator and exactly 89.0 percent after rounding. Confirm 12 complete intervals, 720 covered seconds, matching miss and foreign totals, and `investigate` without an active lookup. An unexpired lookup row must preserve the base-report result as `approved_test` and suppress only the alert derivative.

The boundary fixture adds 450 hits and 50 misses per node per interval, producing exactly 90.0 percent and no result. Test each guard independently rather than combining failures: counter decrease, boot UUID change, 181-second gap, 11 complete intervals, 719 covered seconds, 999 denominator pages, absent node, inconsistent `expected_node_count`, any classified collector error, malformed UUID, null counter, and a value above the exact-integer maximum. Preserve source events, dispatch bounds, job IDs, report output or zero-output, and the lookup revision. This review specifies expected static arithmetic but did not run these scenarios in a Splunk runtime; a runtime reviewer should record the tested Splunk, forwarder, kernel, and numactl versions.

For host acceptance, capture before-and-after sysfs values around an owner-approved representative workload and compare their differences with indexed node deltas. If the default `numastat` utility is available, capture it in the same test window. Inspect `/proc/<pid>/numa_maps`, effective CPU and memory-node constraints, and the launch policy for a known process only after the host-level result establishes a lead. Do not exhaust production memory, rebind a service, migrate pages, or alter policy merely to force an alert.

## Step 5 — Operationalize, investigate, and retain evidence

Build the trend, result, fleet, and health panels described in `visualization`. Restrict saved-search, alert, and lookup modification to the platform operations role; dashboard consumers need read access only to in-scope hosts. Review baselines after kernel, firmware, hypervisor, vNUMA, memory hotplug, scheduler, container policy, or collector changes. Keep approved-test rows visible in the report and apply retention according to the operational evidence policy rather than claiming that this observability use case satisfies an audit requirement.

When a row appears, first establish telemetry integrity: inspect sample age, complete intervals, covered seconds, expected nodes, foreign/miss gap, recent boot, source errors, and the latest raw counters. Then decide whether the host aggregate warrants per-node analysis. Identify workloads active during the exact evaluation window, compare node memory pressure and free-memory context, inspect explicit NUMA/cpuset policies, and correlate with application latency or throughput. A low hit percentage is a placement or capacity lead. Any rebinding, policy change, memory migration, or capacity action requires workload-owner review and rollback planning.

For no events, execute the script as the forwarder user, inspect the boot-ID and sysfs visibility in that service's mount namespace, use `btool` to verify the effective stanza, confirm index routing and forwarding, and search `splunkd.log` for the exact script path. `no_numastat_nodes` can be legitimate on a non-NUMA guest; remove that host from the expected population rather than fabricating counters. `memoryless_or_unqualified_topology` requires topology review, not a collector bypass.

For raw events with null fields, confirm the exact `linux:numastat` spelling and search-tier `KV_MODE`. For merged node lines, correct `SHOULD_LINEMERGE` where parsing occurs. For duplicate minute samples, find overlapping script stanzas by `source` and deployment app. If all ratio rows disappear after reboot or a counter decrease, consult the health view: one transition is intentionally rejected and the rule needs 12 new complete intervals before it can qualify again. If manual and SPL ratios disagree, compare deltas over identical endpoints, retain page units, include all qualified nodes, and use `numa_hit+numa_miss` as the denominator. Do not compare lifetime sums, average percentages, or substitute `local_node+other_node`.

Retain the report and alert definitions, scheduler history, raw baseline/evaluation samples, effective configuration, collector hash, source comparisons, topology qualification, control-test outputs, threshold decision, exception revisions, and exported result rows named in `evidence`. Document gaps explicitly. Runtime behavior, performance causality, and SME approval remain unverified until a qualified operator executes and signs the tests.
grandmaExplanation: We watch whether a large computer keeps placing newly requested memory in the part it preferred. If that success rate stays low, the team can investigate how work and memory are arranged before making risky changes.
hardware: Linux bare-metal hosts or virtual machines that expose one or more regular-memory NUMA nodes through `/sys/devices/system/node/node*/numastat` and `meminfo`. Virtual NUMA must accurately represent the guest topology. Hosts with any detected memoryless node, changing node membership, unreadable node file, or unsupported counter layout remain outside the alert population until separately qualified.
scriptExample:
```sh
#!/bin/sh
PATH=/usr/bin:/bin
export PATH
LC_ALL=C
export LC_ALL

event_version=1
collector=numastat_counter_v1
boot_id=$(sed -n '1p' /proc/sys/kernel/random/boot_id 2>/dev/null || true)
if ! printf '%s\n' "$boot_id" | awk '/^[0-9a-fA-F]{8}-[0-9a-fA-F]{4}-[0-9a-fA-F]{4}-[0-9a-fA-F]{4}-[0-9a-fA-F]{12}$/ {ok=1} END {exit !ok}'; then
    printf 'event_version=%s collector=%s event_type=collector_error collection_status=error error_code=invalid_boot_id\n' "$event_version" "$collector"
    exit 0
fi

discovered_node_count=0
qualified_node_count=0
for path in /sys/devices/system/node/node[0-9]*/numastat; do
    [ -e "$path" ] || continue
    discovered_node_count=$((discovered_node_count + 1))
    meminfo=${path%/numastat}/meminfo
    mem_total_kb=$(awk '$1=="Node" && $3=="MemTotal:" && $4~/^[0-9]+$/ && $5=="kB" {print $4; exit}' "$meminfo" 2>/dev/null || true)
    case "$mem_total_kb" in
        ''|*[!0-9]*) ;;
        *) [ "$mem_total_kb" -gt 0 ] && qualified_node_count=$((qualified_node_count + 1)) ;;
    esac
done

if [ "$discovered_node_count" -eq 0 ]; then
    printf 'event_version=%s collector=%s event_type=collector_error collection_status=error error_code=no_numastat_nodes boot_id=%s\n' "$event_version" "$collector" "$boot_id"
    exit 0
fi
if [ "$qualified_node_count" -ne "$discovered_node_count" ]; then
    printf 'event_version=%s collector=%s event_type=collector_error collection_status=error error_code=memoryless_or_unqualified_topology boot_id=%s discovered_node_count=%s qualified_node_count=%s\n' "$event_version" "$collector" "$boot_id" "$discovered_node_count" "$qualified_node_count"
    exit 0
fi

for path in /sys/devices/system/node/node[0-9]*/numastat; do
    [ -e "$path" ] || continue
    node_dir=${path%/numastat}
    node=${node_dir##*/node}
    if [ ! -r "$path" ]; then
        printf 'event_version=%s collector=%s event_type=collector_error collection_status=error error_code=numastat_unreadable boot_id=%s numa_node=%s expected_node_count=%s\n' "$event_version" "$collector" "$boot_id" "$node" "$qualified_node_count"
        continue
    fi
    awk -v version="$event_version" -v collector="$collector" -v boot_id="$boot_id" -v node="$node" -v expected="$qualified_node_count" '
      $1=="numa_hit"       && $2~/^[0-9]+$/ {value["numa_hit"]=$2}
      $1=="numa_miss"      && $2~/^[0-9]+$/ {value["numa_miss"]=$2}
      $1=="numa_foreign"   && $2~/^[0-9]+$/ {value["numa_foreign"]=$2}
      $1=="interleave_hit" && $2~/^[0-9]+$/ {value["interleave_hit"]=$2}
      $1=="local_node"     && $2~/^[0-9]+$/ {value["local_node"]=$2}
      $1=="other_node"     && $2~/^[0-9]+$/ {value["other_node"]=$2}
      END {
        required[1]="numa_hit"; required[2]="numa_miss"; required[3]="numa_foreign"; required[4]="interleave_hit"; required[5]="local_node"; required[6]="other_node"
        for (i=1; i<=6; i++) if (!(required[i] in value)) missing=1
        prefix="event_version=" version " collector=" collector " boot_id=" boot_id " numa_node=" node " expected_node_count=" expected
        if (missing) {
          printf "%s event_type=collector_error collection_status=error error_code=missing_or_nonnumeric_counter\n", prefix
        } else {
          printf "%s event_type=node_sample collection_status=ok topology_status=qualified numa_hit=%s numa_miss=%s numa_foreign=%s interleave_hit=%s local_node=%s other_node=%s\n", prefix, value["numa_hit"], value["numa_miss"], value["numa_foreign"], value["interleave_hit"], value["local_node"], value["other_node"]
        }
      }
    ' "$path"
done
```
